segments.title: Personifying navies to explain treaty negotiations
segments.summary: Treating navies as characters reveals the pressures hidden behind formal treaty language.
segments.body: The skit began as a seminar exercise about the informal conversations surrounding historical negotiations. Students struggled to imagine the sidebar discussions behind formal treaty language, while a real historical exchange would have given them too much of the answer. Personifying entire institutions lets budgets, force structure, and political pressures shape what each character can plausibly say. The later jokes then work as compressed arguments about what each navy needed, feared, and might have said away from the conference table.

evidence.note: Clarke describes using the personified-navies skit to help students think through side conversations in treaty negotiations.

segments.title: Five treaty navies meet after Washington
segments.summary: The skit assembles the British, American, Japanese, Italian, and French navies to expose why none regards the treaty as a simple triumph.
segments.body: The skit puts the five principal Washington Naval Treaty navies in the British Embassy bar after the politicians have left for official parties. Jokes about British beer and French wine separate the imagined institutional conversation from the conference's formal diplomacy. The Royal Navy, US Navy, Marine Nationale, Regia Marina, and Imperial Japanese Navy arrive after a treaty widely presented as a success, yet all five look dejected. Their shared gloom shows how one settlement could create a different strategic, financial, or political disappointment for every participant.

evidence.note: The scene introduces the Royal Navy, US Navy, Marine Nationale, Regia Marina, and Imperial Japanese Navy after the treaty.

segments.title: The Royal Navy sees a floor against Treasury cuts
segments.summary: Britain's navy treats treaty limits as protection against deeper peacetime cuts rather than permission to build up to the ceiling.
segments.body: The personified Royal Navy expects the Treasury to reduce defense spending as soon as no immediate enemy can be named. It therefore reads the treaty ratio as a floor that might prevent further reductions, not merely as a ceiling on new construction. The joke turns an international arms limit into an internal argument against unilateral economy. The same treaty number can mean protection to one navy and deprivation to another.

evidence.note: The Royal Navy character hopes the treaty will prevent the Treasury from cutting the fleet any further.

segments.title: Paper parity becomes Congress's maximum
segments.summary: The US Navy fears Congress will mistake nominal equality with Britain for a fully funded fleet suited to American distances.
segments.body: In the skit, the American navy argues that a treaty ceiling Britain can use as a minimum will become a maximum in Congress. Formal capital-ship equality may satisfy lawmakers on paper while leaving the fleet without the cruisers it needs. Its existing destroyers are also portrayed as too short-ranged for the missions expected of them. The complaint distinguishes headline tonnage parity from a balanced fleet able to operate across American distances. Treaty arithmetic therefore becomes a question of appropriations, ship types, and endurance.

evidence.note: The US Navy character contrasts paper equality with congressional reluctance to fund cruisers and adequate destroyer endurance.

segments.title: Japan's treaty ratio meets army rivalry
segments.summary: The Japanese navy's complaint combines inadequate fleet strength with a violent domestic struggle against the army for policy and resources.
segments.body: The Imperial Japanese Navy character dismisses British and American budget complaints because its own officers face both spending pressure and political violence. The character describes an army that competes for funding, threatens naval officers, and overlooks the maritime dependence of an island nation. The smaller treaty allocation is presented as insufficient for the navy's tasks, compounding those domestic pressures. The exchange connects dissatisfaction with the Washington ratio to interservice rivalry rather than treating it as a purely international grievance. The result is an arms-control settlement entangled with civil-military conflict inside a participant state.

evidence.note: The Japanese navy character describes army rivalry, threats to officers, budget competition, and too few ships for its tasks.

segments.title: Italy loses the Francesco Caracciolo promise
segments.summary: Italy's comic victory speech mourns the battleship program meant to demonstrate that the Regia Marina and Italian industry had arrived.
segments.body: The Regia Marina calls the settlement a glorious but hollow victory because the Francesco Caracciolo-class ambition will not be realized. The planned battleship stands for Italy's claim that its engineers, industry, and navy had arrived among the great powers. British and American characters quietly undercut the boast by pointing to foreign machinery and equipment within the project. The joke exposes the international industrial dependencies behind a national prestige program. Cancellation costs Italy both the hull and the technological statement it was supposed to make.

evidence.note: The Regia Marina character laments the lost Francesco Caracciolo program while the others note foreign machinery and equipment.

segments.title: French parity frustration and the Béarn conversion
segments.summary: France resents being limited alongside Italy after wartime devastation, while salvaging one consolation through an aircraft-carrier conversion.
segments.body: The Marine Nationale character stresses that France emerged from the First World War badly damaged yet received the same capital-ship allocation as Italy. In the character's lament, the treaty curtails the new battleships and cruisers meant to rebuild French naval strength. The principal consolation is the conversion that became Béarn, chosen from the available hulls because it had turbines and might gain speed after armor removal. The scene shows why nominal parity could feel unequal when participants entered the settlement with different wartime losses and construction prospects. A cancelled battleship program also creates an experimental path into carrier aviation.

evidence.note: The French navy character objects to parity with Italy and identifies an aircraft-carrier conversion as the principal surviving opportunity.

segments.title: Treaty comedy as strategic perspective-taking
segments.summary: Comic institutional voices test the competing realities beneath a formal naval treaty.
segments.body: Students and academics found the caricatures disturbingly recognizable because each complaint grows from a real institutional problem. The method asks viewers to consider what the Washington settlement felt like to each navy instead of treating the signed ratios as the whole story. Budgets, force requirements, political pressures, and industrial limits give each personified navy a coherent point of view. The question, "what was it really like?", frames the skit as historical perspective-taking. Dramatization exposes competing realities that formal treaty language can hide.

evidence.note: Clarke reflects on why students and academics found the institutional caricatures recognizable and historically useful.

segments.title: The Second London Treaty and the illusion of peace
segments.summary: A later skit has Britain, France, and the United States question arms limits while military threats are already unmistakable.
segments.body: The personified-navies idea returns for the London naval treaty system. After the Second London Naval Treaty, the British, French, and American characters ask why their governments keep signing limits while guns are pointed at them and bombs are already falling. Their complaint contrasts the diplomatic desire to preserve an appearance of peace with a naval assessment that the security environment is worsening. The comedy becomes darker as arms limitation moves from postwar retrenchment toward a rearmament crisis. The later skit provides a bridge from Washington to the increasingly fragile treaty system of the 1930s.

evidence.note: Clarke describes a later skit in which the British, French, and American navies question the illusion of peace after the Second London Naval Treaty.

segments.title: Historical teaching through options and context
segments.summary: A closing reflection frames teaching as helping learners see credible alternatives rather than prescribing a single route.
segments.body: The closing reflection begins with the habit of checking how students are doing and remembering what they say. A lecturer's role is to point adults toward help and outline possible approaches while leaving decisions to them. When someone is working through a crisis, the immediately visible route can obscure other workable options. An experienced teacher can step back, raise alternatives, and discuss constraints the learner may not yet have explained. The same habit of widening perspective helps learners see choices and pressures hidden behind an official treaty outcome.

evidence.note: Clarke explains his approach to teaching by presenting options, context, and support while leaving decisions to adult learners.
